hook.text: In 1788, Europeans brought rats to Australia. They've been devouring native wildlife ever since.

buildup.text: Invasive species arrive by ship, plane, or intentional introduction — then explode unchecked.

discovery.text: Without natural predators, invaders outcompete, eat, or infect native species into oblivion.

twist.text: Brown tree snakes in Guam wiped out 10 of 12 native forest bird species after World War II.

climax.text: Invasive species are the second biggest cause of extinction worldwide after habitat loss.

punchline.text: One stowaway can unravel an island's entire web of life.

quiz.question: What is the second biggest cause of species extinction?

details.summary: Invasive species are non-native organisms introduced to new environments where they outcompete, prey on, or disease local wildlife. They are the second leading cause of species extinction globally, costing economies over 400 billion dollars annually.
details.whyItMatters: Globalization moves species across natural barriers at an unprecedented rate. Understanding invasion pathways is critical to preventing irreversible ecological damage.
takeaways: Invasive species are the second biggest extinction driver after habitat loss
Global trade and travel are the primary introduction pathways
Islands and freshwater systems are the most vulnerable habitats

faq.question: Why are islands especially vulnerable to invasive species?
faq.answer: Island species evolved in isolation without exposure to continental predators, competitors, or diseases. They often lack defenses, cannot flee, and have small populations, making them extremely vulnerable when rats, cats, or snakes are introduced.

faq.question: What are some of the most destructive invasive species?
faq.answer: Rats have caused more island extinctions than any other mammal. Cane toads devastated Australian wildlife. Zebra mussels clog North American waterways. And the brown tree snake wiped out most of Guam's native birds.
